The Senate later acquitted him. Hegseth placed the current effort alongside the impeachments of Donald Trump in 2019 and 2021, saying they had failed.

Separately, flight-tracking data showed that the US had withdrawn at least a dozen aircraft, including refuelling tankers, from Mildenhall Royal Air Force base in eastern England on Monday. The Wall Street Journal reported that the move followed a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with events. According to the Journal, as relayed by AFP, the precise nature of that threat was still under discussion among US officials.

The US military said it was taking “coordinated and appropriate” security steps. A spokesperson for its European Command declined to discuss specific force protection measures, noting that various factors can affect them.
items.cav: The Guardian coverage is a live blog and may be updated, and Hegseth’s claims that every strike was lawful are his own assertions, not findings. The Mildenhall withdrawal is second-hand, based on flight-tracking data and unnamed people cited by the Wall Street Journal, and the Iranian threat itself remains unspecified. The BBC material available here is only a summary.
items.op: Whatever one thinks of the Iran war, a defence secretary’s legal justification for it should be tested, not dismissed as a stunt. Calling a congressional challenge sabotage does not answer the questions it raises. Impeachment exists so that claims of lawful conduct are examined in public, and Hegseth’s refusal to engage on the merits weakens that check.

items.t: Former NATO chief says Europe must earn its seat in Ukraine talks, not plead for one
items.s: Former NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen told Euronews that Europe must earn a role in the US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine by offering something useful. He warned that complacency could leave the continent in lasting conflict.
p: Rasmussen argued that Europe is currently in a weak bargaining position and should stop asking for a place among the negotiators. In his view, European governments need to bring capabilities that the talks cannot do without, and he said he hopes they will recognise the urgency now.

He spoke as Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, with the stated aim of ending Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Officials from the EU, NATO, Britain, Germany, Italy and France were also travelling to the United Arab Emirates, but for separate discussions and not the main three-way meeting.

Jared Kushner, an adviser to US President Donald Trump and his son-in-law, said last week that the talks would focus on a new European security order. Russian officials have used similar wording when calling for a smaller NATO presence in Europe. Rasmussen accused Washington of choosing Moscow and siding with Vladimir Putin.

Divisions among European leaders surfaced after the Norwegian prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, held a 90-minute call with Putin. Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen said she was doubtful of the move, which she said had not been coordinated with other leaders.

Rasmussen, a former Danish prime minister, said that speaking to Moscow was sensible in principle, but such initiatives should be planned together. He also rejected the idea that Europe could act as an impartial go-between, saying it would stand with Ukraine.

Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has insisted that eastern European states must have a voice in any settlement, since they face the spillover effects of the war most directly. Asked whether their security concerns should shape the negotiations, Rasmussen said eastern Europeans should have been heard earlier. He led NATO from 2009 to 2014, and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had joined the alliance and the EU in 2004, just before his tenure.

Rasmussen also faulted Washington for holding up approval of US-made air-defence missiles for Ukraine. Zelenskyy said in late October that he had waited nearly a month for Patriot and NASAMS deliveries, and Rasmussen called the holdup a serious blow to Ukraine’s defences. Asked whether NATO had ever been this divided, given US troop cuts, Trump’s threats to leave the alliance and the dispute over Greenland, he said no. He still expects the United States to help Europe in a crisis, but argues that Europe must make its own decisions whoever is in the White House.
items.cav: Rasmussen’s views are his own. Comments attributed to Frederiksen, Sikorski and Kushner are reported second-hand in the article. Zelenskyy’s account dates from late October, and the sources do not say whether the missile approvals have since been granted.
items.op: Europe’s leverage over Ukraine’s future will come from coordinated decisions, not petitions. Leaders who call Moscow without consulting their partners undercut that position. Influence built on unity is the only kind likely to outlast shifts in Washington.

items.t: Lawyers for Rui Pinto open talks with UK authorities on possible cooperation deal
items.s: The legal team of Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto is negotiating with British authorities about a deal that could see him help uncover financial and sporting crime in the UK. The Serious Fraud Office has reportedly made the first approach.
p: Lawyers for Rui Pinto are holding discussions with British authorities on a possible cooperation arrangement. Under it, the man known as the Manchester City whistleblower would help investigators look into serious financial and sporting wrongdoing in the UK, according to the Guardian.

The Guardian says it obtained information showing that the Serious Fraud Office reached out to Pinto after word spread that he was ready to support British investigators, provided he received protection in return. William Bourdon, a lawyer for Pinto who has also acted for Edward Snowden and Julian Assange, confirmed to the newspaper that contact had been made. He said the process was moving forward but gave no further specifics.

Pinto, who is 38, gathered tens of millions of sensitive files between 2015 and 2019. If a deal is struck, he could become a major source for inquiries into financial crime linked to football, law firms and powerful business figures. He might also help officials spot possible tax offences and other irregularities that could otherwise escape detection.

The bulk of the material is currently held by French authorities, who had earlier tried to bring him into a witness protection scheme. Those plans were derailed when Portuguese police arrested him in Hungary in January 2019, yet France has kept in touch with him.

His own position in Portugal is also in doubt. On 30 September he was told that state protection would end after six years. Officials said there was no danger to his life, but advised him to stay out of public debate on contentious topics, avoid crowded places and limit time with relatives. The move was put on hold once it became clear he had never been able to contest it, and he has lodged an appeal that is still pending.

Pinto’s disclosures have reached into Cristiano Ronaldo’s tax affairs, the proposed breakaway European Super League and a number of contested financial deals. Documents he leaked later fed into the Premier League’s inquiry into Manchester City, which concluded the club had breached financial rules.

In 2023 a Portuguese court handed him a suspended four-year prison sentence for attempted extortion and cybercrime. Two years later he was cleared in a second case with similar charges. The public prosecutor and Benfica, one of the clubs he hacked, have challenged that acquittal, and a higher court has yet to rule. Pinto’s backers describe him as a whistleblower who exposed corruption, while his critics say his methods broke legal and ethical norms. He was also the source behind Luanda Leaks, which laid bare the business empire of Isabel dos Santos, who has denied corruption allegations.
items.cav: The deal is still under negotiation and its terms are unknown. Bourdon gave no details, and the Guardian’s account rests on information it obtained rather than on an official announcement. The outcome of Pinto’s protection appeal and the Portuguese challenge to his acquittal remain pending.
items.op: A whistleblower who may help expose wrongdoing should not be left at the mercy of shifting protection decisions. Portugal’s decision to end Pinto’s protection without first giving him a chance to respond undermines trust in the system. Any British agreement must be transparent and bound by clear rules.

items.t: Oil falls to lowest since August as Trump says Iran war is “effectively over”
items.s: Crude prices slid to their weakest point since late August, lifting European and London equities, after President Donald Trump played down the chance of new strikes on Iran. Airlines and other fuel-sensitive shares led the gains.
p: Brent, the international benchmark, dropped almost 3% to $89.66 in early Tuesday trading, its cheapest level since 31 August. The decline followed a slump of roughly 6% the previous day, which traders linked to signs that the fighting could be winding down.

Speaking at the White House, Trump argued that Israel and Gulf partners were adequately shielded from Iranian threats and that there was no need to escalate. He said military action “doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing” at present, while adding that American forces remained ready to act for any reason.

Across Europe the Stoxx 600 rose 0.9% to 662.54, close to the peak it touched in early August amid hopes of a Middle East settlement. The FTSE 100 in London added 0.4% to 10,828. Carriers gained as investors anticipated lower fuel costs, with Lufthansa up 1.8% and Air France-KLM up 1.2%. Oil majors BP and Shell were the weakest large stocks, falling 1.7% and 1.5%.

Analyst Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com said markets were extending their recovery after a strong session on Wall Street, but warned that underlying economic and corporate risks had not disappeared. She suggested the Federal Reserve would want further evidence of cooling inflation before changing course. The latest US inflation figures for October were due at 1.30pm GMT.
For motorists, the AA reported on Monday that the average UK petrol price had dropped 5p a litre since early October, to 169.7p, and that wholesale prices pointed to a further 10p cut on the way.
items.cav: The account relies on a market report whose summary is partly cut off, so the wider state of the Iran conflict is not fully clear. Trump’s “effectively over” remark is his own characterisation, and the sources do not show whether any formal end to hostilities has been agreed. The petrol price outlook is the AA’s projection, not a confirmed outcome.
items.op: Falling oil prices are welcome, but investors and voters should not mistake a presidential remark for a settled peace. Governments that talk down the risk of strikes owe the public clear, verifiable terms. Until those exist, markets are pricing hope, and that is a fragile basis for a recovery.

items.t: Trump says Iran war is ‘effectively over’ as Tehran denies planned talks with Washington
items.s: US President Donald Trump said there was momentum toward ending the war with Iran, while keeping open the possibility of new strikes. Tehran denied that any meeting with US officials was being planned.
p: On Monday, at a White House briefing, Trump argued that Iran had been largely defeated militarily, describing it as “effectively over”. He said Washington was content to hold the current position for now, but warned that the US could resume attacks if needed, and he judged such strikes to be unlikely.

Trump met Qatar’s Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, whom he described as a key mediator in the conflict. It was the first time he had received a foreign leader since his party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. Afterwards, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the pair had a productive exchange covering Iran at length.

Trump said Gulf states favoured the present situation over military action, calling the American pressure on Iran a historic naval blockade and pointing to a land operation known as Iron Gate. According to the Euronews report, Iron Gate is a CENTCOM task force that aims to stop advanced weapons, sanctioned goods and illicit money from moving across Iran’s land frontiers and the Caspian Sea. Trump also said all parties accept that Iran must not acquire nuclear arms.

Qatar’s prime minister, who also met Vice President JD Vance in Washington, called the discussions positive. He said the sides had considered how to move forward on negotiations between Washington and Tehran, and he voiced appreciation for progress toward a deal and regional peace.

Iranian officials responded defiantly. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X that the US was thrashing about in desperation and urged Washington to drop what he called invented reports of talks. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said no such meeting was in preparation. Citing a senior security official, the Tasnim news agency reported that Tehran’s negotiating stance had not shifted and that it would not engage with the US until Washington took concrete steps against Iran’s seven demands.

Media reports on Monday, relaying remarks from Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, said Qatar would host a Vance–Rezaei meeting the following week, which Kalin presented as a chance for a real breakthrough. These claims rest on his account and have not been confirmed by the parties. Meanwhile, Iranian authorities said strikes were still hitting targets, including the island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz. The US military has not publicly confirmed these strikes. Brent crude futures dropped to $92 a barrel on Monday as traders bet the conflict might soon end.
items.cav: The reported Vance–Rezaei meeting comes only from Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin as relayed by media, and Iran has denied it. The strikes in Iran are reported by Iranian authorities; the US military has not publicly acknowledged them. Trump’s claim that Iran is militarily “effectively over” is his own assessment and is not independently verified in these sources.
items.op: Claims that a war is nearly over sit uneasily beside strikes the US military has not publicly acknowledged. Transparency about where force is used, and which talks are really under way, is the least the public is owed before anyone declares victory. Until Washington and Tehran put verifiable facts on the record, optimism should be treated as a hypothesis, not a settlement.

items.t: Trump calls fresh US strikes on Iran ‘highly unlikely’ but says Washington stays ready to act
items.s: President Donald Trump has said renewed American attacks on Iran are improbable, while warning that US forces remain prepared if conditions change. He made the comments after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, amid mounting domestic pressure over the war.
p: Speaking in the White House briefing room on Monday, Trump argued that Iran’s military had been largely neutralised, and said talks aimed at ending the Middle East conflict were moving in a constructive direction. He described Washington’s current posture as a holding pattern, which he said was being maintained largely at the urging of neighbouring states.

The remarks followed an Oval Office meeting with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani. Trump called the talk a productive exchange about bringing the war to a close. Qatar, a US partner in the Gulf and one of Iran’s neighbours, has played a central mediating role. In a message posted on X, the Qatari leader said he had held constructive discussions with Trump and Vice-President JD Vance about a settlement for the region.

Iranian officials have repeatedly questioned Trump’s earlier suggestions that the conflict was close to resolution. According to the BBC, this is not the first time he has described the war as over in military terms, but his political situation has shifted since then. Diplomacy has largely been conducted through intermediaries since the fighting began after joint US and Israeli strikes in February.

The change in tone follows a difficult set of midterm results for the Republicans last week, which senior party figures, including Vance, attributed in part to the war. Before the vote, Trump had acknowledged limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on Sunday, he said he saw no current justification for escalating.

Asked why he had not formally declared the war at an end, Trump said some Gulf partners could still be exposed to Iranian aggression. He suggested that the American naval blockade of Iranian ports was helping to make the region safer. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have all been struck by Iranian fire during the conflict, and the threat of attacks has caused significant disruption to air travel in the region.

Energy markets responded to the developments. Oil prices have dropped sharply since the midterms and fell further after Trump’s remarks. On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude traded more than 1% lower at $91.50 a barrel, while US-traded crude was down 1.2% at $85.82.

The fallout is also reaching the Pentagon. Republican Congressman Thomas Massie intends to bring a House vote this week on impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war. Hegseth, who has Trump’s backing, says he is unconcerned by the threat and Trump has dismissed Massie’s push as a stunt. Because Republicans still hold Congress until January, the motion is unlikely to pass, although Democrats have indicated they would support impeachment once the new session starts.
items.cav: The central claims about Iran’s military position and the state of negotiations come from Trump’s own statements, and Iranian officials have disputed his earlier assessments. The account relies on a single outlet, and the sources do not say what terms a deal might involve or when one could be reached.
items.op: A declaration that a war is effectively over is not the same as ending one, especially when allies and markets remain exposed. Washington owes the public a clear account of what has been agreed, what remains open and who answers for the campaign. Leaders who keep the state of war vague should expect scrutiny from Congress and voters.

items.t: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, under investigation, lobbied Trump on China chip exports, BBC analysis says
items.s: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang is being investigated over an affair involving an alleged Chinese spy, according to BBC analysis by Faisal Islam, who argues he matters more to the future of the world order than other tech leaders. Nvidia shares fell about 4% on Monday.
p: In a BBC News analysis, Faisal Islam compares Jensen Huang with the late Steve Jobs, noting that both are admired innovators with a strong personal presence. Huang, however, is now under investigation over an affair involving an alleged Chinese spy, a matter the piece treats as a serious new risk for the company.

The column explains why Nvidia matters so much. The most advanced systems of today depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years those have been produced by Nvidia, using technology that grew out of graphics hardware and manufacturing capacity in Taiwan. Islam writes that the names of its chips mean little to the public, yet they power the technology that is transforming the world.

Islam met Huang in September last year, during Donald Trump’s state visit to the UK. At the time, Huang was pressing the US government to lift export bans on some of the most capable chips sold to China, including the H200. Islam suggested that Huang was one of the few people who could meet Trump at the White House and then Xi Jinping in Beijing within days. Huang said he believed he had persuaded Trump of his case.

Huang argued that the contest between the US and China is not zero-sum and that American interests were better served if the world relied on US technology. He also said that such computing technology was not a national security concern. Islam notes that many people in national security circles reject this view. They argue that the race for the most advanced technology is effectively zero-sum and that the West, and the US in particular, must act to slow Chinese progress.

The column links those public arguments to the current inquiry. It says the period in which Huang was lobbying is now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage. The piece does not set out the scope of that investigation, who is conducting it, or what it has found so far.

Islam reports that Nvidia shares fell about 4% on Monday, which he attributes to new risks at the point where technology and global politics meet. He says the company is still expected to perform strongly, citing hard revenues of about $400bn this year and a market value of more than $4 trillion.
items.cav: This is an analysis column rather than a news report, and the investigation’s details, the identity of the alleged spy and the status of any findings are not in the source. The revenue and valuation figures are reported without a stated original source, and Huang’s claims are his own, relayed second-hand by Islam.
items.op: Huang’s influence over the chips that shape the future of technology is a matter of public interest, and so is how the inquiry into him is handled. Allegations of espionage against a figure with this much reach call for clear, timely disclosure of what is being examined and why, not market rumour. Until findings are public, the presumption of innocence must hold, and investors and governments deserve facts.

items.t: Trump says FBI is looking into Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.s: US President Donald Trump said the FBI is looking into the relationship between Nvidia’s chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy, as Nvidia’s shares fell. Beijing has rejected the claims.
p: Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI was investigating the affair between Jensen Huang, the boss of chipmaker Nvidia, and a woman US authorities allege is a Chinese spy. Trump said he had spoken to Huang that day and asked him whether he knew the woman was a spy. According to Trump, Huang said he had no idea. Trump said he believed him, though he gave few details of the FBI inquiry and did not say when it had begun. The BBC has contacted the FBI, and the bureau’s response was not reported in the evidence.

The woman is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, who the New York Times reported is a managing director of Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that has had dealings with Nvidia. Citing US intelligence officials, the newspaper said they believe she was spying for Beijing. It also reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to senior officials last spring warning about the relationship. These claims come from the newspaper’s reporting and have not been independently confirmed in the evidence. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related.

China’s foreign ministry rejected the allegations that Huang was targeted, calling them groundless and speculative. Nvidia has said it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security had been compromised, and it has launched an internal investigation. In an email to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted the affair, said he was sorry for hurting his wife and children, and pledged to cooperate with the company’s probe.

Several congressional committees have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s security protocols and his dealings with Megaspeed’s executive. It is unclear whether he will attend. The BBC has contacted Nvidia and the committees, and neither had responded in the reporting provided.

Support for Huang has come from some prominent figures in technology and finance. Elon Musk and investors including Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman publicly defended him, with Maguire describing the affair as a serious mistake and Ackman saying Huang should not get a free pass. Trump also said he believed Huang would stay on as chief executive.

Markets reacted sharply. Nvidia shares fell 4.2 per cent on Monday, closing at their lowest level since 7 April, as investors questioned Huang’s future. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies and is central to the current tech boom, and its chips are at the heart of US export restrictions on sales to China. The company’s standing with regulators and lawmakers may now depend on what the FBI and Congress find.
items.cav: The FBI inquiry is confirmed only by Trump’s own remarks, and the evidence gives no details of its scope. The claims that Alice Huang spied for Beijing rely on unnamed US officials as reported by the New York Times, and China denies them. Huang’s account of the affair comes through his email and Trump’s retelling of their call.
items.op: Public officials should not be the only source of assurances in a matter touching national security and US export policy. Trump’s word that Huang is honest is not an investigation. Transparency from the FBI, Nvidia and Congress is what will show whether the chip industry’s most important company was truly safe.

items.t: Trump says US war in Iran is ‘effectively over’ and escalation is not needed
items.s: Donald Trump has described the war in Iran as “effectively over”, downplaying fears that Washington would step up its military campaign against Tehran once the midterm elections were done.
p: Donald Trump has told reporters that the conflict with Iran has essentially ended, pushing back against expectations that the United States would intensify its campaign after the midterms, according to The Guardian.

Speaking at a White House press conference, Trump argued that Israel and Gulf allies were well shielded from Iranian threats and that new strikes were not necessary for now. He nonetheless said American forces were positioned and prepared to act for any reason.

His comments came after a meeting in the Oval Office with the Qatari prime minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. Qatar has joined other Gulf states in urging Washington not to restart hostilities. The Guardian reports that the Qatari leader spoke of progress toward ending the conflict within a short timeframe, though the summary does not make clear whether that remark was his or Trump’s.
The outlet also points out that Trump has repeatedly suggested a final peace agreement was close, doing so dozens of times over a war that has now lasted close to nine months.

US troop deployments to the region continued in the weeks before the vote. Some commentators speculated that the administration was holding off on renewed fighting until after the ballot to avoid a political backlash. Republicans then suffered a heavy defeat, losing control of both chambers of Congress, and Vice-President JD Vance publicly blamed the Iran war as a major factor.

Earlier in the day, Trump posted on Truth Social that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait would favour keeping the current arrangement, which he described as a long-running naval blockade. He reiterated that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon and said Washington could return to full-scale operations if conditions changed, while calling such a move unlikely.
items.cav: This account rests on a single outlet, and the sources do not describe the negotiations, the terms under discussion or conditions on the ground. It is also unclear from the summary whether the “fairly soon” remark came from Trump or from the Qatari prime minister, although the headline attributes it to Trump.
items.op: A claim that the war is “effectively over” should be tested against facts, not applause, especially from a leader who has repeatedly predicted an imminent deal. Before the public accepts that fighting has ended, the administration should set out plainly what has been agreed, what remains unresolved, and what would trigger renewed strikes. Transparency is the only real test.

items.t: Republican congressman moves to force House impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
items.s: Representative Thomas Massie plans to bring impeachment articles against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to a House vote this week, a step widely expected to fail. Massie says his aim is to prompt President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats take control of Congress.
p: Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky formally filed articles of impeachment against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Monday, according to the BBC. He accuses Hegseth of breaching the US Constitution.

Massie argues that Hegseth has been waging hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without authorisation from Congress, and says that makes the defence secretary answerable under the law. Asked why he was pressing ahead, Massie told reporters he was acting on principle.

Few observers expect the effort to succeed, since Republicans keep their majorities until January. Massie's stated goal is to push Trump into dismissing Hegseth before Democrats can open an impeachment inquiry of their own.

Hegseth struck a dismissive tone. He said he was unconcerned, and told reporters he would hold a news conference on Tuesday morning on the subject. The BBC notes that his previous news conference took place in May.

Massie lost his re-election bid earlier this year. He has been a vocal critic of Trump and of the Iran conflict, which began almost nine months ago, and he has also pressed the administration to release federal files on Jeffrey Epstein. The articles, as reported, accuse Hegseth of intimidating critics of the administration, of seizing foreign leaders and of disregarding War Powers resolutions. The BBC did not independently verify these allegations.

Once the resolution is filed, House Speaker Mike Johnson has to set a date to take it up within two days. Members may vote on it outright, send it to committee, or shelve it. House Democrats look likely to support it, and their leader Hakeem Jeffries said he would be a firm supporter. Massie himself said he was unsure there were enough votes to pass it.

Peter Loge, a public affairs professor at George Washington University, told the BBC that the measure could clear the House because the Republican margin is so narrow, and that some frustrated Republicans may stay away from the vote. Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University, said impeachment has become more frequent as American politics has grown more polarised, and predicted several more of Trump's cabinet members could face it.

Removing a cabinet secretary requires approval by both chambers. The House has impeached only two cabinet members in US history, and the Senate convicted neither. A conviction needs two-thirds of senators, a bar Democrats would not reach in January without Republican votes. Gowder suggested the current Senate could confirm a replacement if Hegseth left before the new session, while Loge said Hegseth's chances of serving out Trump's term are slim.
items.cav: The allegations are Massie's claims as set out in the articles, and the BBC report does not confirm them. Hegseth's only response in the sources is that he is unconcerned, and the content of his planned news conference is not described. The expected outcome is also contested, as Loge expects the House to pass the measure while Massie is unsure it has the votes.
items.op: Serious accusations against a cabinet secretary deserve a full, transparent process, not a rushed vote aimed at getting ahead of a rival party. Congress should test the claims on the record, and Trump should explain publicly how he will address the questions the articles raise.

items.t: Steel plant blast in western Turkey kills at least 17 workers
items.s: At least 17 people have died and more were hurt after an explosion and fire at an iron and steel plant in Aliaga, near Izmir in western Turkey. Officials say the blast followed a crane accident during work at the site.
p: The explosion happened around midday at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, a port district of Izmir province. According to the BBC, the victims were all workers at the facility, one of Turkey’s leading steel producers. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the plant and a tall column of smoke.

The Izmir governor, Süleyman Elban, said a crane carrying a replacement boiler had collapsed, sending materials into a furnace below. Euronews, citing President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s televised address, reported the same sequence. The company that runs the plant said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance on one of its electric arc furnaces.

Casualty figures have shifted. Erdoğan first put the death toll at 16. Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu later said one critically injured person had died, raising the total to 17. The number of injured is reported differently: the BBC gives 12, while Euronews gives 13, including two in critical condition.

Elban told reporters that some people were believed to still be trapped under the rubble, and search and rescue work continued. Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay said on X that teams were working to remove the collapsed platform.

Erdoğan confirmed the deaths after a cabinet meeting and said investigations were under way. He said the circumstances, including whether there was negligence and who bears responsibility, would be established. The BBC’s Turkish service, citing local media, reported that at least five people had been arrested. Those arrests have not been confirmed by the authorities in the sources available.

The Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society group, said workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey. Euronews described the Habas group as privately owned, and said the plant was founded in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel a year, according to the company’s website. That capacity figure comes from the company itself and has not been independently verified in these reports.
items.cav: The sources differ on the number of injured (12 or 13) and on the arrests, which rest on local media reports relayed by the BBC. The cause is described by officials and the company, and the investigation has not yet reported findings.
items.op: When workers die in an industrial blast, the public is owed a clear account of who inspected the equipment and who approved the work. Investigators should publish their findings, and any negligence should be answered for under the law, not left to a statement of regret.

items.t: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang admits affair as board opens national security probe
items.s: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted an affair after reports that he may have been targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The company’s board has launched an independent investigation, and analysts say his position could be at risk.
p: For more than three decades, Jensen Huang has been the public face of Nvidia, which he co-founded in 1993 and grew into one of the most valuable chipmakers in the world. He has also kept the company close to his family, with his children Madison and Spencer holding senior roles and his wife, Lori Mills Huang, running the family foundation, which is reported to control more than 60 million Nvidia shares as of 2024.

That image was badly damaged this weekend. The New York Times reported at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset with whom he had developed a close relationship. In a letter to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that he had been having an affair.

The Times reported that US officials had suspected Huang of helping to smuggle American chips into China and had monitored Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean datacentre firm Megaspeed. According to the reporting, officials allegedly concluded during that surveillance that she was a Chinese spy and had become close to the Nvidia leader. Earlier, a company spokesperson had said there was nothing out of the ordinary about his interactions with her. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment before publication.

In his letter, Huang said he supported the investigation, wrote that he took full responsibility for the hurt he had caused, and apologised to his family. Nvidia’s board has now launched an independent inquiry into the national security concerns linked to the relationship.

Analysts and investors quoted in the report said Huang could be removed as chief executive depending on the outcome. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives described it as a “black eye moment” that could prompt congressional inquiries and weigh on the share price. Ken Mahoney of Mahoney Asset Management compared Huang’s role at Nvidia to that of Steve Jobs at Apple, while warning that the bigger question was whether a successor could keep the company’s strategic direction.

Nvidia shares fell 7.5% at the opening of the market, wiping out more than $330bn in value, according to the report. Andy Challenger of Challenger, Gray & Christmas argued that the case was about judgment and national security exposure, not only personal morality.

In a statement, the board said it did not believe national security or company secrets had been compromised, and it expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team, while promising further updates as appropriate.
items.cav: The account of the alleged spy and surveillance comes from New York Times reporting as relayed by the Guardian, and the Guardian did not independently confirm it. Megaspeed had not responded, and the board’s finding that no secrets were compromised is a preliminary statement, not the outcome of the investigation. The talk of Huang’s possible removal is analysts’ speculation.
items.op: A company’s leadership should not hinge on one executive’s private life, but when that life touches a national security inquiry, shareholders and the public are owed more than reassurance. The board’s independent investigation should be published in full, with its findings open to scrutiny. Confidence statements are no substitute for transparency.

items.t: Nvidia shares fall after board opens investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.s: Nvidia’s share price dropped about 4% on Monday after the chipmaker’s board said it would investigate chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman US officials reportedly believe was a Chinese spy. Beijing has rejected the claims.
p: Nvidia’s market value fell sharply on Monday, with the stock down roughly 4% at the close, after the company said its board would run an independent inquiry into chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The BBC put the loss in market value at about $250bn (£190bn).

The probe followed press reports suggesting Washington believed Huang had been singled out in a Chinese espionage effort. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair, calling himself “unfaithful” and apologising to his wife and children. He said he remained committed to protecting the company and supporting US national security, and pledged to cooperate. Nvidia said it had no reason to think its secrets or national security had been compromised.

According to a New York Times report cited by the BBC, American intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, worked for Beijing. She ran Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm that has done business with Nvidia. The same account says Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to senior officials last spring, cautioning that the chief executive had a close bond with a Chinese agent. The BBC noted that these assertions are not independently verified in the material it had.

Beijing has dismissed the accusations, with its foreign ministry calling them baseless and designed to besmirch China. On Capitol Hill, members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee have asked Huang to attend a private briefing about his contacts with Alice Huang and about how Nvidia guards against espionage. Three lawmakers, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, wrote that the reports raise serious concerns about Chinese access to sensitive American technology and that Congress must establish how far national security may have been put at risk.

Other prominent tech executives, Elon Musk among them, have publicly backed Huang remaining in charge. Analysts quoted by the BBC expected the setback to fade. Victoria Fernandez of Crossmark Global Investments said investors were unlikely to desert a company so vital to the sector building hardware for emerging technologies, though she noted Nvidia has no obvious heir to Huang.

Governance is the sharper question. The BBC reported Huang holds only about 3.5% of the company, and because Nvidia has a single class of voting shares, that stake would not give him a veto over a board decision to remove him. That contrasts with founders such as Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, who hold substantial stakes across several share classes. Fernandez doubted the board would move against Huang without clear evidence of wrongdoing linked to national security or intellectual property, though she expected a possible number two to be identified. Savers are also exposed: pensions and savings in index-tracking funds holding Nvidia can move with its share price.
items.cav: The affair and the espionage claims come from a New York Times report that the BBC relayed, and the sources do not show independent confirmation of Alice Huang’s alleged role. China has denied the allegations, and Nvidia has not said what the investigation will examine or when it will report.
items.op: A chief executive’s private conduct is his own business, but when it may intersect with alleged espionage, shareholders and lawmakers have a legitimate claim to facts. Nvidia’s inquiry should be genuinely independent and its findings published in full. Investors should not be reassured by a share price rebound; transparency must decide whether Huang stays.

items.t: Massie pushes for a House impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
items.s: Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie has filed eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, opening the way for a possible House vote this week. The step follows months of criticism of Hegseth over the Iran war and other military operations.
p: Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman from Kentucky who is leaving office and has frequently clashed with President Donald Trump, has pressed for a House vote to remove Pete Hegseth. According to The Guardian, Massie charges that the defense secretary waged war without congressional approval and misused the authority of his office.

Speaking on the House floor, Massie told colleagues that Hegseth had committed “high crimes and misdemeanors” and had carried out unlawful orders. The Guardian reports that Massie is expected to attract some Republican votes. Under House rules, a vote would have to be held by Wednesday at the latest.

Massie first filed the articles on 15 September. Speaker Mike Johnson then adjourned Congress before the measure could be considered. Republicans will keep their House majority until newly elected members are sworn in during January.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House who is widely tipped to become speaker, has described himself as a “hard yes” on impeachment. In an interview with ABC News on Sunday, he said Hegseth needs to leave his post.

On Monday, Hegseth addressed the Naval War College and unveiled changes to military training, arguing they would help officers wage war swiftly and with deadly precision. Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other Republican figures have blamed their heavy losses in last week’s midterm elections largely on the Iran conflict and its impact on household finances.

Hegseth answered his critics in a brief video posted on Thursday, calling the impeachment push an attempt at personal ruin and saying it would fail against him. The watchdog groups Common Cause and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington contend that the video breaches the Hatch Act, which limits the use of public money for partisan purposes.

Massie’s resolution lays out further charges. It asserts that Hegseth bypassed Congress’s constitutional power to declare war through unauthorised strikes on Iran and Yemen. It also cites the deaths of more than 100 children at a school in Iran and accuses him of ordering suspected drug boats in the Caribbean sunk without rescuing their crews. The document further contends that the investigation and threatened prosecution of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, over calls for troops to refuse illegal orders, violated the First Amendment, and it describes the alleged kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as unlawful.
items.cav: The sources do not confirm whether the House vote will happen or how many Republicans will support it. The allegations, including the claim about child deaths in Iran and the legality of the Maduro operation, come from Massie’s resolution and are not independently established in the reporting.
items.op: Impeachment is a grave remedy and should turn on whether an official broke the law, not on who is politically inconvenient. If Congress believes Hegseth acted without authorisation, it should weigh the evidence in public and vote on the record. Delaying the question again would tell voters that accountability depends on party loyalty.

items.t: Jensen Huang’s affair raises questions about Trump’s response to intelligence warnings
items.s: The Nvidia co-founder has admitted an affair with a Chinese businesswoman said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. The Guardian’s editorial board argues that the White House’s failure to act on warnings demands an explanation.
p: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman. According to the Guardian, she is said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. The paper describes the case as something close to a spy thriller, given Huang’s status as one of the most powerful figures in the technology boom.

According to the editorial, Donald Trump was briefed on the relationship and took no action. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “No, I don’t think so.” The paper suggests that he may have seen the matter as a private breach of marriage vows, or that he chose to overlook it.

The editorial links the episode to Nvidia’s growing influence in Washington. Huang is described as a backer of Trump’s datacentre expansion, a donor to the White House ballroom project, and an ally in opposing safeguards on the technology. The Guardian says Nvidia’s chips, which became central to the race for tech supremacy, also became a national security issue once China joined the competition.

The paper recounts that the US imposed export controls on GPU sales to China in October 2022, and that Nvidia was effectively barred from selling to Beijing about thirty months later. It says Huang lobbied for looser rules, and that the White House then scrapped Biden-era global chip restrictions and allowed sales of Nvidia’s H200 processors to Chinese customers.

The Guardian reports that Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company whose executive was Ms Huang, was investigated in 2025 over suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. Analysts at Culper Research argued in May that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenue, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. The editorial also says that more than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation once Wall Street opened.

According to the paper, reports suggest the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia contacted investigators. The editorial says Democrats, encouraged by their midterm success, are likely to seek answers, and that Congress has grounds to examine whether the administration knowingly set aside a foreign intelligence threat.

The editorial places the case within a longer history. It notes that diplomatic or military honeytraps have traditionally been more common than commercial ones, and that British intelligence agencies accused Beijing in 2008 of using sex to pressure businesses. The paper states that whether this has happened in the Huang case is unknown.
items.cav: This is an editorial opinion, and its account of the intelligence claims is second-hand: the paper says Alice Huang is “said to have” passed intelligence to Beijing. The report that the commerce probe was halted rests on unnamed reports, and the editorial does not confirm whether any honeytrap took place.
items.op: Whether a chipmaker’s lobbying shaped national security policy is a question of public trust, not partisanship. If the president knew of a possible security risk and chose inaction while easing export rules, Washington owes the public a full and transparent explanation.

items.t: Nvidia shares fall as investigation opens into reports CEO was targeted by Chinese intelligence
items.s: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation after reports that chief executive Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, a claim China denies. Shares fell in premarket trading as the story spread.
p: Nvidia said it was launching an independent investigation following reports that its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been the target of “a foreign intelligence effort”. According to the reports, that effort led to a romantic relationship between Huang and a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, who had allegedly been recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Huang has admitted an affair. In a statement he said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family. He also said he was “fully committed to Nvidia” and would work to earn back employees’ confidence. China has denied the spying claims.

Alice Huang reportedly worked for Megaspeed, a datacentre company based in Singapore. Megaspeed has been suspected of routing Nvidia chips to China and evading export controls, though the reporting cited in the evidence does not establish that as fact. Jensen Huang has publicly criticised US export controls on advanced chips, arguing in May 2025 that they had been a failure.

The Financial Times reported that Alice Huang and a business partner, Kang Wei, sought investment in early 2025 for a south-east Asian data centre project worth several hundred million dollars. According to two investors, the pair said they had “no problem securing GPUs” and cited Alibaba as a client. A US hedge fund had claimed six months earlier that Alibaba secretly funded Megaspeed.

Markets reacted quickly. Nvidia ended last week worth $4.5tn, and shares were down around 6% in premarket trading, with more than $200bn potentially wiped from its value once Wall Street opened. Asian markets were recovering, with Japan’s Nikkei up 2.2% and Taiwan’s TAIEX up almost 5%. Elon Musk publicly backed a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that criticised Huang’s conduct.

Separately, Bloomberg reported that Alphabet is rolling out a broader range of its tensor processing units, custom chips used to develop and run software, which adds to competitive pressure on Nvidia. Prediction market Polymarket put the chance of Huang resigning or being removed by the end of the year at 15%.
items.cav: The espionage link rests on reports and claims, not on any confirmed finding, and the investigation’s outcome is not yet known. The Alibaba funding claim comes from a hedge fund’s allegation made months earlier, and the investor accounts are second-hand. Market figures are premarket and may change.
items.op: Whatever the facts of this affair, the public interest is in an independent inquiry that is transparent about its findings. Nvidia’s investors and the wider public deserve clear answers on export controls and on who was able to reach its chief executive. Speculation should not substitute for evidence.

items.t: Cop31 opens in Antalya as UN warns heat is building faster and the US stays away
items.s: Climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, opened as the World Meteorological Organization reported that heat is building up in Earth's systems at a faster pace. The United States, which has withdrawn from the international climate framework, will again send no official delegation.
p: The UN’s weather agency said the gap between the energy Earth receives from the sun and the energy it sends back has reached its largest level since measurements began. Releasing its global climate update as the summit got under way, it said 2026 was on course to rank among the four hottest years ever recorded.

According to the agency, average surface temperatures from January to September 2026 ran about 1.47C above the preindustrial level. Monthly sea surface temperature records were broken, and sea levels stood at their highest since record-keeping started. Oceans take in roughly 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and 2026 is on track to be the tenth straight year of record ocean heat.

The agency warned that this heat build-up will intensify extreme weather, including heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the world had moved into an era of severe climate extremes, pointing to a strong El Niño event layered on top of human-caused warming. He added that the people who have done least to cause the problem are suffering most.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister, is presiding over the negotiations in Antalya. Our colleague Adam Morton questioned him about the apparent contradictions in Australia’s record: a country with high emissions is leading the talks while still exporting fossil fuels and approving projects that add pollution.

Young activists at the summit also made their case. Janiely Truká, an Indigenous activist and poet from Brazil who advises Unicef Brazil on youth issues, said that for Indigenous communities the climate crisis threatens their way of life, their traditional knowledge and their future generations. She called for firm funding commitments, protection of Indigenous territories and easier access for young people to these negotiations.

The United States will again have no official government presence at the summit, the second year running. A White House official said the administration would not send anyone and criticised the summit for ignoring what it sees as the damage done by extreme climate policies. About 20 members of Congress travelling to Antalya have been refused the usual State Department support and are relying on philanthropic money. Democratic congressman Sean Casten, who is attending, described the situation as outrageous.

A recent UN report found that the US was the one major economy that did not cut or slow its carbon pollution last year, adding an extra 133m tons of planet-warming gases from coal, oil and gas. President Donald Trump has previously dismissed climate action as a scam. Finance is expected to be the most contentious issue, with developing countries pressing for money that wealthier nations would rather keep off the agenda.
items.cav: The temperature and ocean figures come from a World Meteorological Organization update covering only January to September, so they are provisional. Several claims about the US and the summit come from live coverage and from quotes given by officials and lawmakers, and the sources do not independently verify them. The article does not say what outcomes the talks are likely to produce.
items.op: Transparency at these summits matters as much as ambition. Delegates should publish agendas and funding arrangements early, and governments that talk about climate finance should show the money. Vague promises from any capital, including the host, will not protect the people already paying the price.

items.t: Kraków shooting: Polish prosecutors widen probe as attacker dies in hospital
items.s: Six people were killed when a gunman opened fire in Kraków’s main square over the weekend, and the 24-year-old Polish attacker has since died in hospital. Authorities say the investigation will continue to determine whether he acted alone.
p: Polish investigators opened a terrorism case after a gunman from Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a town in southeastern Poland, fired on people in the city’s central square on Saturday afternoon, according to the Guardian’s live coverage. Six people lost their lives, one of them a Briton, and 17 others were wounded. Authorities later said the assailant, who had been hit during an exchange of fire with officers, died in hospital.

A national day of mourning was declared for the first of two planned days. Police said the bodies of three relatives were found at the attacker’s home: his father, 53, his mother, 52, and his 21-year-old sister. Among the wounded were nationals of Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia, as well as two police officers, one of them in serious condition.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect had been drawn to far-right ideas and held “very radical” views. Those remarks were later softened, and nationalist opposition figures challenged the basis on which they had been made. Government spokesperson Adam Szlapka urged restraint in commenting while the initial signs remained unconfirmed.

According to interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka, Poland’s cybercrime bureau, CBZC, has detained five people over online posts praising the shooter. She warned that officers were on heightened alert for possible copycat attacks.

Justice minister Waldemar Zurek said the probe would proceed despite the attacker’s death, with a focus on whether the gunman worked alone. The square reopened on Sunday evening after the security cordon was removed.
items.cav: The account comes from a live blog that relays official statements and has not been independently verified. The interior minister’s ideological claims were partly walked back and their basis has been disputed, so the suspect’s motive remains unclear. The sources do not say what the five detained people are suspected of or whether the posts led to charges.
items.op: A rare mass shooting in a city centre demands facts, not early labels. Poland’s government was right to pull back from a motive it could not yet support. Transparency now means publishing what the investigation establishes, including whether anyone helped the gunman, and treating the detained suspects with the presumption of innocence.

items.t: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang admits affair as reports link his companion to alleged Chinese spying
items.s: Nvidia's chief executive has admitted an extramarital affair after US media reports said the woman involved was suspected of spying for Beijing. The company has opened an independent investigation.
p: Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the chipmaker Nvidia, has acknowledged an extramarital affair. On Sunday he said he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologised for the hurt caused to her and their children. He also said he would cooperate with an internal security investigation.

The affair is with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman who is not related to him. According to a New York Times report, which the BBC cites, US intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by China’s top intelligence agency and was spying for Beijing. Her current whereabouts are unknown. She did not respond to a request for comment from the newspaper.

Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm that had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia says it investigated those concerns and found them to be unfounded. The BBC understands that Megaspeed is now under investigation by the Singapore government over earlier claims that it evaded US sanctions on exports of Nvidia’s high-end chips.

The New York Times reported that surveillance captured communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was later identified as Jensen Huang. It remains unclear what intelligence, if any, she gathered and passed on. Nvidia told the BBC it was not aware of any intelligence concerns, and said it trusted the US government would have warned it of a genuine threat. China has rejected the allegations as “groundless”.

The reports have a political dimension. According to the New York Times, Donald Trump was briefed last year on intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was spying for China. Asked whether he wished he had acted on it, Trump said he did not think so and called Huang “an honourable guy”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment, though the newspaper reported that he had overseen a memo last spring warning the administration about the relationship.

The stakes are high because Nvidia sits at the centre of the contest between the US and China over the most advanced technology. Export controls introduced since 2022 have largely shut the company out of the Chinese market, and Huang has pursued talks between Washington and Beijing in an effort to win back access. The affair, the reports suggest, may have complicated his hopes of a broader approval to sell more advanced chips to China.
Huang, born in Taiwan in 1963, co-founded Nvidia after working at AMD. Bloomberg’s billionaires index estimates his fortune at $155bn.
items.cav: Much of the espionage detail is second-hand, drawn from a New York Times report that the BBC relayed, and Alice Huang has not commented. What intelligence she may have passed to Beijing is unknown, and Nvidia’s claim that US national security was not compromised has not been independently verified.
items.op: The question is not Huang’s marriage but whether a company central to national security was kept properly informed. Officials who held intelligence about his associate owe lawmakers and the public a clearer account of what was known and what was done. Reassurance from either Nvidia or the administration is no substitute for transparency.
